1:
Henry gives five reasons why the place was fixed rather than chosen: it had to be at Jerusalem, where God had put his name; on Mount Moriah, which some think the very spot where Abraham offered Isaac in Genesis 22:2; where the Lord had appeared to David and answered him by fire, so that atonement having been made there once it must still be made there; in the place David had prepared, not only purchased but pitched on by divine direction, so that it was Solomon's wisdom not to enquire out a more convenient one; and in a threshingfloor, which he turns into a lesson, that temple-work requires the labour of the mind as threshing does that of the body, its Jebusite owner giving encouragement to the Gentiles. Clarke supplies the Targum, which has Abraham praying and worshipping there, Jacob praying there as he fled from Esau, and the angel of the Lord appearing to David.

Ellicott notes that nowhere else in the Old Testament is the site so specified, and finds an etymology behind it. Where the Lord appeared unto David should be who appeared unto David, the name Moriah being taken to mean the appearance of Jah, so that the verse reads in the mount of the Appearance of Jah, who appeared unto David his father. He rejects the Latin, which makes the mount one shown to David, since the verb never means to be shown or pointed out, and notes that the Syriac, misunderstanding the Greek, produced the hill of the Amorites; the clause about the place David prepared he thinks has suffered an accidental transposition.

On the date Ellicott finds a scribe's error: the Hebrew reads in the second month in the second, which the versions do not repeat, and since on the second day would be put differently the line should read simply that he began to build in the second month. Henry is interested instead in the three years before, not trifled away but spent in preparation, and passes on a conjecture that this was a sabbatical year, when a people released from husbandry could lend a hand, the year of finishing falling out to be another. The next clause divides them. Henry and Wesley keep the received sense, that Solomon was instructed, Wesley adding by David and by the Spirit of God; Ellicott and Delitzsch agree independently that the words are not about instruction at all but mean this is the foundation, or ground-plan, of Solomon, both taking the plural pronoun as a neuter singular and the infinitive substantively.

The last notes are about numbers. On the ancient measure Clarke explains why Chronicles mentions it: the book was written after the captivity, and without the note a reader would assume the Babylonian cubit, a palm shorter than the cubit of Moses. Ellicott and Delitzsch say the same and add that the chronicler has dropped the height given in Kings; Wesley glosses it as the measure first fixed, and Henry draws the lesson that the dimensions were given by divine wisdom, so nothing can be put to them or taken away, and Solomon's first measure is his last. The hundred and twenty cubits of the porch nobody but Wesley will have. Clarke suspects transposed letters, the word for a hundred being the word for a cubit with two exchanged, which yields twenty, agrees with the Syriac, the Arabic and the Alexandrine Greek, and brings the porch within proportion. Ellicott presses the same case further: a hundred and twenty would make the porch four times the height of the house, the Syriac omits the clause, it has no parallel in Kings, and it wants the word cubits, which the numbers here usually carry; he guesses the Hebrew is a corruption of and its breadth ten cubits. Wesley alone lets it stand, taking the porch for a kind of turret to the building.
5:
The panelling needs a gloss and Ellicott gives it: to ciel, or rather seel, meant in old English to wainscot or panel a room, so the great chamber was covered with planks of fir and the wainscoting plated with gold. Delitzsch calls the wood cypress and reads the ornaments as artificial palms set on the walls, the chains being a spiral decoration, garlands of flowers carved on the wainscot. Ellicott agrees the chain-work must have been garland-like carving on the fir panels, notes that the parallel in Kings omits it, and lines up the versions: the Greek has palms and chains, the Syriac the likeness of palms and lilies, the Latin palms and, as it were, chainlets intertwining.

The precious stones divide them over what surface is meant. Delitzsch takes them for ornament of the inner sides of the walls and calls the claim very easily credible, since Solomon brought such stones in quantity from Ophir and it was a common custom in the East to employ them in buildings and vessels. Henry has them set here and there where they would show to best advantage, remarks that the finest houses now pretend to no better garnishing than good paint while these were substantially rich, and reads them as a type of the new Jerusalem, which has no temple in it because it is all temple. Ellicott records that the Latin explains the phrase instead as a floor of costly marble, and Clarke prints that rendering in full without deciding between them.

Parvaim gets four answers and nobody is confident. Delitzsch says the name occurs nowhere else and has not been satisfactorily explained, then reports that Gesenius compares a Sanskrit word for first or foremost and takes it for the eastern regions, while others make it a city in Arabia through which Indian gold reached Palestine. Ellicott offers an auriferous region in southern Arabia, allows the same Sanskrit derivation for those who seek it in India, and notes that the name does not recur in the Old Testament. Clarke canvasses two more: that it is Sepharvaim, and that it is Taprobane, now Ceylon, the name derived by Bochart from a word for border, the coast of Parvan. He adds the rabbinic answer, that the gold was of a blood-red colour and took its name from the word for heifers, being like bullocks' blood.

The nails divide them too. Ellicott reads the Hebrew as a weight for nails, fifty shekels in gold, and holds with the Greek and the Latin that this is the weight of each nail, since fifty as a total would be a trifling sum to record beside six hundred talents. Clarke will not have it: bolts must be intended, since it would be preposterous to suppose nails of nearly two pounds' weight. Henry and Wesley take a third way, that each nail weighed fifty shekels or rather was worth so much, workmanship and all. Ellicott then supplies the corroboration the others lack: whatever is thought of the quantities of gold David is said to have amassed, plating on this scale is well attested from the monuments. Nebuchadnezzar records clothing the shrines of his temple with gold and the oracle's cedar roof with bright silver, and Esarhaddon a century earlier boasts of castles made to shine like day with silver and gold.

The upper chambers are read three ways. Clarke thinks the ceiling is probably meant and Wesley says rather the roof, while Ellicott takes them for the chambers over the holy of holies mentioned elsewhere in Chronicles, adding that both statements of the verse are peculiar to this book and that the Syriac and Arabic omit it. On the six hundred talents he supplies the figure that makes the sum felt: Solomon's whole yearly revenue was six hundred and sixty-six talents, and the weight is not given in Kings at all.
10:
Henry explains why two more cherubim were wanted when two already stood over the ark. Those were small, and being appurtenances of the ark, which alone of the tabernacle furniture was not made new, they continued; but the most holy place was now enlarged, and the large pair were added, doubtless by divine appointment, to fill a room that would otherwise have looked bare and unfurnished. What image work means is less settled. Delitzsch calls it sculpture work from a root meaning to form or fashion. Ellicott renders it literally a work of statuary, observes that the Hebrew word occurs here only and looks suspicious, and sets the versions against it: the Latin has statuary work, the Greek a work of logs, the Syriac a durable work, the last three agreeing with the blocks of oleaster named in Kings, so that the original reading may have been simply woodwork. Wesley takes it another way again, as moveable work, not fixed to the mercy seat like the cherubim of Moses but in a moving posture.

Which way the figures looked is a plain contradiction. Henry has their faces inward toward the ark, and builds on it: had they been set there to be adored they would have been made sitting, as on a throne, with their faces toward their worshippers, whereas standing on their feet with faces to the ark shows them attendants on the invisible God. Ellicott translates the same word toward the chamber, and states flatly that these cherubs did not face each other as the pair on the mercy seat did. Henry draws the doctrine either way: we must not worship angels but must worship with angels, having come into communion with them, and the thought that we worship him before whom the angels cover their faces will help inspire reverence in every approach to God.

On the wings the two who measure agree. Ellicott works the arithmetic out, each wing five cubits and each cherub therefore covering ten of the chamber's twenty, so that the inner wing of the one met the inner wing of the other in the middle while the outer wings touched the walls. Delitzsch reads the repeated clauses as distributive and reaches the same arrangement. Henry adds a reading of his own to the veil's cherubim, that the Hebrew says he caused them to ascend, which means either that they were made in raised work, embossed, or that they were made on the wing in an ascending posture, where the other two stood on their feet in an attending posture, so as to remind the worshippers to lift up their hearts and soar upwards in their devotions.

The veil is the one item here that Kings does not have, and all four notice it. Delitzsch observes that it is absent from the parallel and that it was made of the same materials and colours as the veil of the tabernacle, inwoven with similar cherub figures. Ellicott adds that although Kings omits the curtain it does speak of the chains of gold from which the veil was probably suspended, and that what is meant here is raised figures in tapestry or broidered work, the description in Exodus 26:31 being identical. Henry and Wesley read it alike and theologically: the veil denoted the darkness of that dispensation and the distance at which the worshippers were kept, but at the death of Christ it was rent, so that through him we are made nigh and have boldness not only to look but to enter into the holiest.
15:
The height of the pillars is the chapter's last number problem and it gets three answers. Delitzsch and Ellicott both hold that eighteen cubits is right, since Kings and two other places give it, and both account for the thirty-five here as corruption: Delitzsch by the confusion of two similar pairs of Hebrew numeral letters, Ellicott by noting that the Greek and the Latin read thirty-five while the Syriac and Arabic read eighteen. Henry needs no emendation at all, taking the thirty-five and somewhat over as the two pillars measured together, which leaves about eighteen cubits apiece and agrees with the other accounts without touching the text. On the chapiter the two who gloss it agree: Ellicott calls it the capital, literally the ornament, where Kings says the crown, and Delitzsch derives the word from a root meaning to overlay and makes it the hood of the pillar.

The chains produce the sharpest textual disagreement in the chapter, because the received Hebrew puts them in the oracle, and the passage is about pillars standing outside the house. Delitzsch says the phrase has no meaning there and emends the word to collar, a decoration on the capital, noting that the Syriac and Arabic took the other course and paraphrased chains of fifty cubits, as though they ran out of the most holy place to the pillars. Ellicott refuses that emendation although he grants that most commentators have made it and that the change is very slight. He alters the preposition instead, an infinitesimal change in Hebrew writing, which yields chainwork as in the chancel; and he defends the sense on the ground that although the chronicler has not said the walls of the holy of holies were so ornamented, he said it of the great hall, and Kings declares the whole house adorned with mural carvings, so that the comparison was natural to write. He adds that the Greek plainly had the present text and, not understanding it, simply transliterated the two Hebrew words.

On the capital's furniture the two technical voices fill each other out. Delitzsch describes it in two parts, the lower a rounded swell covered with chain-like network a cubit high, set with carved pomegranates in a row above and a row below. Ellicott supplies the arithmetic that the hundred pomegranates here conceal: from Kings it appears there were four hundred altogether, an upper and a lower row of a hundred each on the chainwork of each pillar.

The names draw out what the pillars were for. Wesley translates them, Jachin that he shall establish and Boaz that in it is strength; Henry reads the same pair as establishment and strength in temple-work and by it. Clarke prints the Targum, which makes Jachin commemorate the establishing of the kingdom of the house of David and takes Boaz from the patriarch of the family of Judah from whom all the kings of Judah descended. Ellicott ends the chapter by defending the chronicler's competence. Reuss had called this description, much more detailed in Kings, almost unintelligible under the pen of the abbreviator, and the disputed word absolutely unintelligible and foreign to the text; Ellicott answers that the first is a strong exaggeration and the second a hasty decision, and had already asked at the earlier verses why the sketch of the porch and nave should be called confused at all.
